section.title: Contend with Those Who Contend
section.sectionRationale: An imprecatory lament of David, appealing to the LORD as both warrior and judge to contend with those who repay his kindness with betrayal and hate him without cause, a phrase Jesus applies to His own rejection in John 15:25. David's honest cry for justice is not personal vengeance but a plea entrusting judgment entirely to God.
section.thesis: David's plea that the LORD contend with those who hate him without cause, though he had shown them only compassion, is an honest, Spirit-given prayer entrusting justice to God rather than seizing it himself, a pattern of innocent suffering fulfilled in Jesus, hated without cause by those He came to save.
section.frameNote: Six movements: an opening plea that the LORD contend as warrior for him (1-3); prayer for the humiliation of those who plotted evil without cause (4-8); a vow to rejoice in the LORD's salvation (9-10); unjust accusation despite his compassion in their illness (11-16); the cry 'how long, O LORD,' and prayer against those who hate without cause (17-21); and a closing appeal for vindication and a vow of ongoing praise (22-28).

units.label: Contend with my opponents, O LORD
units.note: an opening plea for God as warrior

verses.text: {{riyb|Contend}} with my opponents, O LORD; fight against those who fight against me.
Take up Your shield and buckler; arise and come to my aid.
Draw the spear and javelin against my pursuers; say to my soul: "I am your salvation."

units.label: Without cause they laid their net
units.note: prayer for the humiliation of hidden plots

verses.text: May those who seek my life be disgraced and put to shame; may those who plan to harm me be driven back and confounded.
May they be like chaff in the wind, as the angel of the LORD drives them away.
May their path be dark and slick, as the angel of the LORD pursues.
For without cause they laid their net for me; without reason they dug a pit for my soul.

May ruin befall them by surprise; may the net they hid ensnare them; 
may they fall into the hazard they created.

units.label: My soul will rejoice in the LORD
units.note: a vow to rejoice in salvation

verses.text: Then my soul will rejoice in the LORD and exult in His salvation.
All my bones will exclaim, "Who is like You, O LORD, who delivers the afflicted from the aggressor, the poor and needy from the robber?"

units.label: They repay me evil for good

verses.text: Hostile witnesses come forward; they make charges I know nothing about.
They repay me evil for good, to the bereavement of my soul.
Yet when they were ill, I put on sackcloth; I humbled myself with fasting, but my prayers returned unanswered.
I paced about as for my friend or brother; I was bowed down with grief, like one mourning for his mother.
But when I stumbled, they assembled in glee; they gathered together against me. Assailants I did not know slandered me without ceasing.
Like godless jesters at a feast, they gnashed their teeth at me.

units.label: How long, O Lord
units.note: a cry against those who hate without cause

verses.text:
How long, O Lord, will You look on? Rescue my soul from their ravages, 
my precious life from these lions.
Then I will give You thanks in the great assembly; I will praise You among many people.
Let not my enemies gloat over me {{chinnam|without cause}}, nor those who hate me without reason wink in malice.

For they do not speak peace, but they devise deceitful schemes 
against those who live quietly in the land.
They gape at me and say, "Aha, aha! Our eyes have seen!"

units.label: Vindicate me by Your righteousness
units.note: a closing appeal and vow of praise

verses.text: O LORD, You have seen it; be not silent. O Lord, be not far from me.
Awake and rise to my defense, to my cause, my God and my Lord!
Vindicate me by Your righteousness, O LORD my God, and do not let them gloat over me.
Let them not say in their hearts, "Aha, just what we wanted!" Let them not say, "We have swallowed him up!"
May those who gloat in my distress be ashamed and confounded; may those who exalt themselves over me be clothed in shame and reproach.
May those who favor my vindication shout for joy and gladness; may they always say, "Exalted be the LORD who delights in His servant's well-being."
Then my tongue will proclaim Your {{tsedeq|righteousness}} and Your praises all day long.

riyb.gloss: To contend, dispute, plead a legal case. David asks the LORD to act as both warrior and advocate, taking up his cause the way a defender argues a case in court, a plea for justice rather than personal revenge.

chinnam.gloss: Without cause, for nothing, gratuitously. David's repeated insistence that his enemies hate him without cause becomes, in Jesus's own words, a direct description of His rejection by the world, John 15:25.

tsedeq.gloss: Righteousness, rightness, justice. David's closing vow is to proclaim this quality of God continually, the same righteousness ultimately vindicated when the truly innocent sufferer, Christ, was raised from the dead.

basic.context: David appeals to the LORD as both warrior and legal defender, asking Him to contend with those who plot against him without cause even though he had shown them only kindness, fasting and mourning when they were ill. Betrayed by hostile witnesses and mocked by those gloating over his distress, David cries out, 'How long, O Lord, will You look on,' and pleads for vindication by God's own righteousness, vowing to praise Him publicly once justice is done.
basic.hermeneutics: This imprecatory psalm should be read as honest, Spirit-given prayer that entrusts vengeance entirely to God rather than seizing it personally, echoing Romans 12:19's command to leave room for God's wrath rather than repaying evil directly.
basic.originalLanguages: David asks the LORD to riyb, contend or plead his legal case, against enemies who oppose him chinnam, without cause, a phrase Jesus later applies directly to His own rejection, John 15:25, and vows to proclaim God's tsedeq, righteousness, once vindicated.
basic.typology: David's experience of being hated without cause despite showing only compassion, verses 12-16, 19, anticipates the greater innocent sufferer, Jesus, who was likewise hated without cause by those He came to heal and save, a connection Jesus Himself makes explicit, John 15:25.
basic.christ: Jesus quotes this psalm's language directly, applying David's cry that his enemies 'hate me without reason' to His own rejection by the world: 'the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: They hated Me without cause,' John 15:25. Where David could only appeal to God to contend for him and vindicate him by righteousness, Christ's own vindication came through resurrection, the ultimate proof that the truly innocent sufferer is upheld by God even when hated and betrayed by those He loved.
basic.god: God is shown as both warrior and judge, one who sees every hidden plot and unjust accusation, and whose righteousness is the only sufficient ground for vindicating the innocent sufferer, sparing David the need to take vengeance into his own hands.
basic.crossReferences: John 15:25 quotes this psalm's language directly, applying 'hated Me without a cause' to Jesus's rejection by the world. Romans 12:19 commands believers to leave room for God's wrath rather than avenging themselves, the same posture David models throughout this psalm. Isaiah 53:7 pictures the suffering servant, silent before His accusers, embodying the innocent suffering this psalm describes.
basic.oneStory: David's honest cry that he is hated without cause despite showing only compassion becomes, in Jesus's own words, a description of His own rejection by the world, and just as David entrusted his vindication entirely to God's righteousness, Christ's resurrection is the final proof that the truly innocent sufferer is upheld by God, never abandoned to His enemies' gloating.

context.literary:
Psalm 35 is built in three panels, and each panel ends the same way. Verses 1 to 10 open with a battle cry and close with a vow that the soul will rejoice and the bones will speak. Verses 11 to 18 rehearse the injustice suffered and close with a promise of thanks 'in the great assembly'. Verses 19 to 28 return to the plea and close with a promise that 'my tongue will proclaim Your righteousness'. The psalm is therefore not a straight line from complaint to comfort but a spiral, three times round the same wound, and each time the vow of praise is a little wider, first the inner life, then the assembly, then all day long.

It speaks in the language of three arenas at once. Verses 1 to 3 are a battlefield, with shield, buckler, spear and pursuers. Verses 7 and 8 are a hunter's world of nets and pits. Verses 11 and 23 to 24 are a courtroom, with witnesses, a cause to be pleaded, and a verdict called 'vindicate'. The person praying is at once a soldier, a quarry and a defendant, and the LORD is asked to be a warrior, a trapper turned against the trappers, and a judge.

The psalm also contains a running contest of speech. The enemies charge things the psalmist 'knows nothing about', verse 11, slander him 'without ceasing', verse 15, 'do not speak peace', verse 20, and say 'Aha, aha! Our eyes have seen!', verse 21, and again, 'We have swallowed him up!', verse 25. Against this David sets the single sentence he wants from God, 'I am your salvation', verse 3. Verse 9 answers verse 3, so that the soul which was promised salvation ends by rejoicing in it. The word shalom, peace, forms a frame too: the enemies 'do not speak peace', verse 20, but the LORD 'delights in His servant's well-being', verse 27.
context.historical:
The superscription says only 'Of David', and the psalm does not name its occasion. The best candidates are the years when Saul hunted him, when informers such as Doeg carried tales to the king, 1 Samuel 22:9-10, and David could say to Saul, 'Why do you listen to the words of men who say, "Look, David intends to harm you"?', 1 Samuel 24:9. Another possibility is the rebellion of Absalom, when friends and counsellors turned against him. The psalm's picture of once-loyal people who gloat 'when I stumbled', verse 15, could suit either time, and the poem is written so that many afflicted people could use it.

The legal frame would have been familiar. Israel's law took false testimony very seriously. A malicious witness who accused a man falsely was to be tried before the LORD, the priests and the judges, and given the penalty he had meant for his brother, Deuteronomy 19:16-19. The phrase 'hostile witnesses' in verse 11 belongs to this world, as does the request that the trap they set catch them in verse 8. Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple envisages an accused person coming to swear an oath before the altar so that God will judge, 'condemning the wicked man by bringing down on his own head what he has done, and justifying the righteous man', 1 Kings 8:31-32. Some readers think psalms like this one were used by ordinary Israelites who had been wrongly accused and who brought their case to the sanctuary.

The imagery of the psalm reflects life in the land. Chaff on the threshing floor, the wind that carries it off, the hunter's net and pit, the sackcloth of mourning, and fasting were part of daily life and worship. The figure of the angel of the LORD who drives enemies away recalls the night the angel struck the Assyrian camp, 2 Kings 19:35. The 'great assembly' of verse 18 is the gathered congregation of Israel at the sanctuary, where a vow made in trouble was paid in public, as in Psalm 22:25.
context.canonical:
Psalm 35 belongs to a cluster of prayers of the innocent under attack. Its lines are echoed elsewhere in the Psalter with unusual closeness. Psalm 38:19-20 has 'many hate me without reason' and 'those who repay my good with evil'. Psalm 40:14-15 asks that 'those who seek my life' be ashamed and confounded and that those who say 'Aha, aha!' be appalled, with almost the same words as Psalm 35:4, 21 and 26. Psalm 69:4 speaks of those who 'hate me without cause', and Psalm 109:4-5 speaks of enemies who 'repay me evil for good'. The Psalter treats the situation of the wronged servant as a permanent feature of life under God.

The angel of the LORD appears here as the one who drives away enemies, verses 5 and 6, and in Psalm 34:7 as the one who encamps around those who fear the LORD. The same messenger protects the faithful and pursues their pursuers.

In the New Testament, Jesus applies the language of the psalm to Himself: 'This is to fulfill what is written in their Law: "They hated Me without reason"', John 15:25. He uses 'Law' in the broad sense of Scripture, and the line has its counterparts in this psalm and in Psalm 69:4. The trial of Jesus opens with 'many false witnesses', Matthew 26:59-60, and the mockers at the cross cry 'Aha!', Mark 15:29, as the enemies do in verse 21. The imprecatory psalms were also read by the early church as Scripture with contemporary use, as when Peter cites Psalms 69 and 109 in Acts 1:20. The cry 'How long, O Lord', verse 17, is taken up by the martyrs under the altar, Revelation 6:10, and answered in Revelation 19:1-2.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David wrote so that people who are slandered and betrayed would have words for it. The first thing the psalm does is refuse the two easy responses. It does not tell the wronged to suppress their anger, and it does not tell them to take revenge. Every wish in the psalm, from the shield and spear of verse 2 to the ruin of verse 8, is addressed to God. The prayer places the fight in His hands and asks Him to be the warrior.

He also meant to make the case that the suffering is undeserved, and he does it with evidence: he had mourned for these people in their illness, fasting and putting on sackcloth as for a brother or a mother, verses 13 and 14. The betrayal has weight because of the love that came before it. The passage teaches that innocence does not shield one from hatred, and that loyalty is not always repaid.

The psalm is also a lesson in patient hope. David asks, 'How long, O Lord, will You look on?', and at once vows to give thanks in the great assembly. The vows are not conditions but confessions that the case is safe with God. First hearers were being taught that lament is not the opposite of faith. It is faith with its eyes open, speaking to the God who sees, and turning to praise even before the answer arrives.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records a specific man's prayer at a specific time of danger. Its requests for shame, ruin and a trap that catches the trappers describe what David asked, and they are not commands for every reader to imitate word for word. They belong to a covenant world where public justice was the LORD's business and where the law itself said that a false accuser should receive what he intended for another, Deuteronomy 19:19.

What carries over is the direction of the prayer. Paul says, 'Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath', Romans 12:19, and Peter says, 'Do not repay evil with evil', 1 Peter 3:9. The psalm and those texts point in the same direction: the wronged hands the matter to God. The New Testament adds what the psalm does not say, and it is the command to bless, love and pray for enemies, Matthew 5:44, Romans 12:14, and the example of Jesus, 'Father, forgive them', Luke 23:34.

The descriptive material about David's compassion, verses 13 and 14, is something to imitate: to weep with those who weep, Romans 12:15, even for people who will later turn on us. The psalm should not be used as a script for cursing a particular enemy. It is an honest way to bring injustice to God and to leave it there.

debates.question: Can Christians pray the wishes for enemy ruin in verses 4 to 8 and 26?

views.label: Yes, as prayers for God's justice
views.case: The requests are addressed to God, and they ask for exposure and shame, not personal violence. Paul himself quotes vengeance as belonging to the Lord, Romans 12:19, and the martyrs in Revelation 6:10 ask how long before God judges. On this view believers may pray that God will put an end to wickedness and vindicate the innocent.

views.label: No, the new covenant has replaced them with love of enemies
views.case: Jesus commands, 'Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you', Matthew 5:44, and Paul says, 'Bless and do not curse', Romans 12:14. On this reading the imprecations belong to the Old Testament's framework of earthly justice, and the Christian prayer is that enemies be saved, following Luke 23:34.

views.label: Both, once the wishes are re-aimed at the gospel
views.case: The wicked's shame may be prayed for as the end of their power and the exposure of their lies, but the deepest 'ruin' the Christian asks for is repentance. God's judgment is real, and so is His offer of mercy, and the psalm's cry for justice is transposed by the cross where justice and mercy meet.

debates.bearing: The psalm should not be dropped from Christian prayer, because it teaches that injustice matters to God. Its requests need to be read through the whole Bible: the Christian brings the same grief and hands over the same case, and adds the prayer that enemies be reached by the gospel, which is what the Lord Jesus practised.

debates.question: Is this the prayer of David in one crisis, or a prayer for any accused person in the sanctuary?

views.label: David's own experience
views.case: The superscription names David, and the psalm's first-person detail fits his biography: the kindness he showed, the false reports, the gloating over his stumble. On this view the psalm was written out of Saul's persecution or Absalom's rebellion.

views.label: A liturgical prayer for the falsely accused
views.case: The courtroom language, the appeal to be vindicated, and the vow to give thanks in the great assembly fit a sanctuary setting like the one Solomon describes in 1 Kings 8:31-32. On this reading an accused person prayed the psalm and offered thanks when acquitted.

views.label: Both: David's prayer that became the people's
views.case: David's own experience produced a prayer that was preserved because others could use it, and its wording is broad enough for any innocent sufferer. The Psalter regularly holds personal and communal readings together.

debates.bearing: The third view fits both the superscription and the way the New Testament uses the psalm. Jesus does not treat it as a private diary but as Scripture that speaks of the righteous who are hated for no reason, and that is exactly what it is for.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 3 asks God to say to the soul, 'I am your salvation'. The word is yeshuah, and what David asks is not that God give him a rescue but that God speak Himself as the rescue. It is the same claim Moses makes at the sea, 'He has become my salvation', Exodus 15:2. The name Jesus is a form of the same word, and the Gospel of Matthew explains it: 'He will save His people from their sins', Matthew 1:21. Verse 9 then answers verse 3, as the soul that was promised salvation rejoices 'in His salvation'.

The second half of verse 3 has a translation puzzle. The BSB has 'Draw the spear and javelin', and its footnote notes that the line may also be read 'and close the way'. The Hebrew word after 'spear' is a rare one that could name a weapon or come from the verb to shut. If it is the verb, the LORD is asked to block the road ahead of the pursuers, which fits verse 6, where their path is 'dark and slick'. Either way, the psalm asks God to stop the enemies before they reach him.

The 'hostile witnesses' of verse 11 are literally witnesses of violence, and the same phrase is the legal term for a malicious witness, the kind Exodus 23:1 warns against and Deuteronomy 19:16 has in view. David is using the vocabulary of the Torah, not just complaining. The 'bereavement of my soul' in verse 12 is from the root for losing children, used of Rebekah's fear in Genesis 27:45, and of the loss Babylon feared in Isaiah 47:8-9. Repaid evil for good, David feels like a parent who has lost a child.

The last words of verse 13 are hard. The BSB says 'my prayers returned unanswered', and the footnote gives the literal form, 'returned to my bosom'. Some take it as prayers that came back unheard. Others take it as a wish: if the sick did not deserve his prayer, may it return to bless him. Both readings show a man who prayed for those who hated him.

In verse 17 'my precious life' is the word yechidah, literally 'only one', the word that stands behind Psalm 22:20, 'my precious life from the power of wild dogs'. It is the life that cannot be replaced, and it is set against the lions. Finally, the two uses of shalom, peace, in verses 20 and 27 form the psalm's frame: the enemies 'do not speak peace' to the quiet in the land, but the LORD 'delights in His servant's well-being', a word that means wholeness, not merely safety.

typology.type: The one hated without cause, verses 7, 19
typology.fulfillment: Jesus takes David's phrase as His own: 'They hated Me without reason', John 15:25, and tells His followers that the world hated Him first, John 15:18. The trial confirms it: the Sanhedrin sought false testimony and found none that agreed, Matthew 26:59-60. The escalation lies in who He is. David was hated by rivals, but Jesus was hated by those He came to save, and this hatred led to a cross. The type falls short in the response: David prayed for shame on his enemies, while Jesus prayed, 'Father, forgive them', Luke 23:34.

typology.type: The friend repaid with betrayal, verses 12 to 16
typology.fulfillment: David sat in sackcloth for people who then gloated when he stumbled. Jesus healed all the sick who came to Him, Luke 4:40, and took on Himself our infirmities, Matthew 8:17, yet when He was arrested 'all the disciples deserted Him and fled', Matthew 26:56, and the crowd mocked Him with 'Aha!', Mark 15:29, the very cry of verse 21. Where David's kindness was partial, Christ's compassion was perfect, and where David's friends turned, Christ's turned even as He carried their sin.

typology.type: The trap that catches its makers, verses 7 and 8
typology.fulfillment: The psalm asks that 'the net they hid ensnare them'. Scripture knows this pattern, as when Haman was hanged on the gallows he prepared for Mordecai, Esther 7:10, and Psalms 7:15-16 and 9:15 state it as a principle. It reaches its sharpest point at the cross: 'None of the rulers of this age understood it. For if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory', 1 Corinthians 2:8, and by that death Christ 'disarmed the powers and authorities', Colossians 2:15. The type is not exact, since the powers were overthrown by the very death they inflicted, which is more than a trap turned on its makers.

typology.type: The word 'I am your salvation', verse 3
typology.fulfillment: David asks God to speak a single sentence to his soul. The answer comes in a person. Simeon holds the infant and says, 'my eyes have seen Your salvation', Luke 2:30, and the angel says the child's name is Jesus 'because He will save His people from their sins', Matthew 1:21. What David asked for in words is given in flesh. The type falls short in that David wanted assurance for a threatened life, while the salvation in Christ reaches the root of sin and death.

study.christ:
Jesus says of Himself, 'This is to fulfill what is written in their Law: "They hated Me without reason"', John 15:25. The line comes in the middle of His warning to the disciples that the world will hate them because it hated Him first, John 15:18-19. He is quoting the language of this psalm, and of Psalm 69:4 which shares it, and He means Scripture as a whole by 'their Law'. What He is saying is that the righteous man of the Psalter, hated for no cause, has a name and a face, and that it is His.

The Gospels show how closely the story tracks the psalm. In verse 11 'hostile witnesses come forward; they make charges I know nothing about', and at the trial of Jesus 'many false witnesses came forward' though they found none whose testimony agreed, Matthew 26:59-60. In verse 15 the people 'assembled in glee' when the psalmist stumbled, and the crowd gathered at the cross to mock. In verse 21 they say, 'Aha, aha! Our eyes have seen!', and Mark records passers-by shouting 'Aha! You who are going to destroy the temple', Mark 15:29. In verses 13 and 14 David mourns for the ones who later turn on him, and Jesus healed every sick person who was brought to Him before He was handed over.

The psalm leads to Christ also by contrast, and this is where its deepest turn lies. David asks that the wicked be put to shame and their net ensnare them. Jesus, hated without cause, does not pray that curse on His enemies. He prays, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing', Luke 23:34. And in dying He takes the curse on Himself: 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us', Galatians 3:13. The ruin the psalm calls down on those who hate without cause falls, at the cross, on the one who was hated without cause, and He bears it for the haters, 'when we were enemies of God', Romans 5:10.

The psalm's cry for vindication also finds its answer in Him. David asks, 'Vindicate me by Your righteousness', verse 24. Paul says Jesus 'was declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead', Romans 1:4, and an early Christian hymn says He 'was vindicated by the Spirit', 1 Timothy 3:16. The tongue that David vowed would proclaim God's righteousness all day long, verse 28, is picked up by the church, which proclaims the righteousness of God revealed in Christ.

A word of caution: Jesus is not every 'I' of the psalm. The prayers for shame and ruin, verses 4 to 8 and 26, and the claim to have done no wrong to his enemies, verses 11 to 14, are David's own, and David is a sinner, Psalm 143:2. The psalm points to Christ where the innocent sufferer speaks, and the New Testament supplies the boundaries.
study.god:
Psalm 35 shows a God who is asked to do three things at once, to fight, to plead and to judge, and it assumes He can. The opening words call Him warrior, with shield and spear, and advocate, contending for David's cause. This is not a small view of God. The LORD is not a bystander who watches injustice from a distance but a party to it, who takes the side of the poor and needy 'from the robber', verse 10. The psalm's confession, 'Who is like You, O LORD', echoes the song at the sea, 'Who among the gods is like You, O LORD?', Exodus 15:11, but here the incomparable one is praised for rescuing the weak.

God sees. 'O LORD, You have seen it', verse 22. What people hide, the net set in secret, the pit dug 'without reason', the slander from 'assailants I did not know', is not hidden from Him. This is a comfort for the wronged and a warning for the wrongdoer, and the psalm holds both.

God is also asked to be moved. The psalm asks Him not to be silent, not to be far off, to awake and rise. That is bold language, and it appears elsewhere in the Psalter, as in Psalm 44:23, 'Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping?' The psalm does not think God has fallen asleep, but it knows how it feels when He seems slow. 'How long, O Lord, will You look on?' asks the question that faith is allowed to ask.

God's righteousness is the ground of the case. David does not say, 'Vindicate me because I deserve it', although he insists he is innocent of this charge. He says, 'Vindicate me by Your righteousness', verse 24, and 'my tongue will proclaim Your righteousness', verse 28. The whole appeal rests on who God is. Elsewhere David prays, 'Do not bring Your servant into judgment, for no one alive is righteous before You', Psalm 143:2, so that his innocence toward these enemies never becomes innocence before God.

He is a God who delights in the peace of His servants, verse 27, which is a striking way to speak of the Almighty. The one who acts in judgment is at heart the one who wants His people well. Justice serves shalom, and shalom is what the enemies refuse to speak.

The tension the psalm leaves open is that God's justice is real but not yet done. He sees, and yet the psalmist must ask Him to act. This is the shape of faith between the promise and its fulfilment, and the answer comes in the Bible's last chapters, where 'His judgments are true and just' and He 'has avenged the blood of His servants', Revelation 19:2. For worship, the psalm teaches us to bring wrongs to God as the right court of appeal, to praise Him in advance for a verdict not yet given, and to trust that the one who delights in our peace will not leave the case unheard.

crossReferences.note: The angel of the LORD 'encamps around those who fear Him' in Psalm 34, and in Psalm 35:5-6 the same angel drives their enemies away like chaff. The two psalms sit side by side and show the angel protecting the faithful and pursuing those who pursue them.

The law of the malicious witness requires that both parties stand before the LORD and the judges, and that a proven liar receive what he intended for his brother. David's 'hostile witnesses', verse 11, and his prayer that the trap catch its makers, verse 8, assume this principle of fitting justice.

Solomon's prayer envisages a man who swears an oath before the temple altar and asks God to judge, condemning the wicked and justifying the righteous. It offers a likely setting for a prayer like Psalm 35, the appeal of an accused person to the LORD as judge.

Another prayer of the innocent, with 'those who hate me without cause outnumber the hairs of my head'. Together with Psalm 35:19 it lies behind John 15:25, and shows that the phrase 'without cause' belongs to the Psalter's general portrait of the righteous sufferer.

These verses share phrases with Psalm 35: those who seek my life be ashamed and confounded, those who say 'Aha, aha!' be appalled at their shame. Psalm 70:3 repeats the cry. The repetition suggests the Psalter treats these words as a shared prayer for people under attack.

Psalm 35:10 asks 'Who is like You, O LORD?', taking up Israel's song at the sea. The incomparability of God, first shown in rescuing a slave people from Pharaoh, is here applied to the rescue of a single poor man from the aggressor.

The chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin seek false testimony against Jesus, and many false witnesses come forward. The scene is the hostile witnesses of verse 11 in action, and shows the innocent sufferer of the psalm standing in the dock.

Passers-by heap abuse on Jesus with 'Aha!' The exclamation is the same malicious glee the psalm records twice, in verses 21 and 25. Mark's readers, who knew the psalm, would have heard David's enemies in the mouths of the crowd.

From the cross Jesus says, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.' It is the answer to the psalm's imprecations: the hated one hands the case to God and asks for mercy on the haters. It is where the psalm's prayer for justice meets the gospel.

Paul tells believers not to avenge themselves but to leave room for God's wrath, and to feed a hungry enemy. It states the ethic that the psalm practises, handing the wrong to God, and then adds what the psalm does not, the positive command to do good to enemies.

The martyrs under the altar cry, 'How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood?' It is the cry of verse 17 given to the whole company of the wronged, and Revelation 19:1-2 records the answer, so that the psalm's prayer is heard at the end of the story.

study.oneStory:
The first murder in the Bible is the murder of a man who did nothing to earn it. Cain 'rose up against his brother Abel and killed him', Genesis 4:8, and John explains that he did it 'because his own deeds were evil, while those of his brother were righteous', 1 John 3:12. Psalm 35 belongs to the line that begins there: the righteous hated without cause, and the God who hears the blood crying from the ground. Joseph's brothers 'hated him and could not speak a kind word to him', Genesis 37:4, and the same pattern runs through Israel's story, through prophets, through David running from Saul, and through the psalmist who sits in sackcloth for people who have decided he is their enemy. The fall did not just break the relation to God. It broke the peace between people, so that shalom is now something enemies 'do not speak', verse 20.

The psalm's answer is not violence but a case brought to God. It is a prayer that turns the fight over to the LORD, who at the sea had already shown Himself as warrior and rescuer of the weak, Exodus 15:11. It assumes a God who sees, who will not stay silent forever, and who delights in the well-being of His servants. In that way the psalm keeps alive, through the long years of injustice, the conviction that the world has a Judge.

The story reaches its turning point when the one hated without reason comes Himself. Jesus quotes the psalm's own words about Himself, John 15:25. Facing false witnesses and the mockers' 'Aha!', He takes the curse that the wronged might have called down on their enemies and, in bearing it, offers those enemies forgiveness, Luke 23:34 and Galatians 3:13. Vindication comes on the third day, Romans 1:4, and His people are told to expect the world's hatred as His were, John 15:18-19, and yet to bless and not to curse, Romans 12:14.

The story ends with the answer to the psalm's questions. The martyrs' 'How long, O Lord?' is met with the shout of a great multitude, 'His judgments are true and just', Revelation 19:2, and the wrongs of history are put right. The 'great assembly' in which David vowed to give thanks becomes 'a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue', Revelation 7:9, and the peace that the enemies refused to speak is what the redeemed live in forever, for 'He will wipe away every tear from their eyes', Revelation 21:4.

quiz.q: What imagery does David use in verses 1-3 to describe his plea to God?

options.text: Both courtroom and battlefield imagery, asking God to contend as his advocate and fight as his warrior.
options.note: David combines legal and military language, asking the LORD to take up shield and spear on his behalf.

options.text: Only military imagery, with no legal or courtroom language.
options.note: Close, since battle imagery, shield and spear, is prominent, but the opening verb 'contend' also carries specific legal, courtroom overtones alongside the military language.

options.text: Only agricultural imagery of planting and harvest.
options.note: The imagery here is military and legal, not agricultural.

options.text: Imagery of a wedding celebration.
options.note: The opening imagery concerns conflict and legal defense, not celebration.

quiz.q: How does David say he treated his enemies when they were ill, according to verses 13-14?

options.text: He put on sackcloth, fasted, and mourned for them as for a close friend or family member.
options.note: David describes genuine compassion shown to those who later betrayed him.

options.text: He felt sympathy privately but took no visible action.
options.note: Close, since sympathy is part of the picture, but David describes active, visible practices, sackcloth and fasting, not merely private feeling.

options.text: He ignored them completely.
options.note: David describes active mourning and fasting on their behalf, not indifference.

options.text: He publicly celebrated their suffering.
options.note: David's response was mourning and intercession, not celebration of their suffering.

quiz.q: What phrase in verse 19 does Jesus later apply directly to Himself in John 15:25?

options.text: 'Those who hate me without reason.'
options.note: Jesus quotes this language directly to describe His own rejection by the world.

options.text: 'My precious life from these lions.'
options.note: While vivid, this is not the specific phrase Jesus quotes; the direct quotation concerns being hated without cause.

options.text: 'They repay me evil for good.'
options.note: Close in theme, since both phrases describe unjust treatment, but the exact wording Jesus quotes in John 15:25 is 'hated Me without a cause,' from verse 19, not the 'evil for good' language of verse 12.

options.text: 'They gape at me and say, Aha, aha!'
options.note: This is not the phrase Jesus quotes; the direct quotation is about being hated without cause.

quiz.q: What does David ask God to do in verse 24?

options.text: Vindicate him by God's own righteousness, and not let his enemies gloat over him.
options.note: David appeals specifically to God's righteous character as the ground for his vindication.

options.text: Simply remove him from the situation without addressing the accusers.
options.note: Close, since relief is desired, but verse 24 specifically asks God to actively vindicate him by righteousness and stop the enemies' gloating, not merely to remove him from the circumstance.

options.text: Remove him from public life entirely.
options.note: The request is for vindication and God's active defense, not withdrawal from public life.

options.text: Punish David for his own past failures instead.
options.note: The request concerns vindication against false accusers, not self-punishment.

quiz.q: What does David vow to do once vindicated, according to verse 28?

options.text: Proclaim God's righteousness and praises all day long.
options.note: The psalm closes with a vow of continual, public praise once vindication comes.

options.text: Give thanks privately, without any public declaration.
options.note: Close, since gratitude is the underlying attitude, but verse 28 specifically vows public, ongoing proclamation, 'my tongue will proclaim,' not private, silent thanks.

options.text: Seek out his enemies to personally punish them.
options.note: The closing vow is about praise, not personal retaliation against enemies.

options.text: Remain silent about what God has done.
options.note: The vow is explicitly to proclaim, not to remain silent.

questions: David shows genuine compassion, fasting and mourning, for enemies who later betray him. Have you ever been mistreated by someone you had genuinely cared for, and how did you respond?

This imprecatory psalm entrusts vengeance entirely to God rather than seizing it personally. Where in your own life are you tempted to take justice into your own hands rather than trusting God's timing and righteousness?

Jesus applies this psalm's words, 'hated without cause,' directly to His own rejection. How does knowing that Jesus experienced the same kind of unjust hatred you may face change the way you process being wrongly treated?

David cries, 'How long, O Lord, will You look on?' in the middle of ongoing injustice. What situation in your life currently tempts you to ask God this same question, and how are you bringing that honestly to Him?
David vows to praise God publicly once vindicated. What would it look like for you to praise God now, in the middle of unresolved injustice, rather than waiting until every wrong is made right?

translationNotes.note: Contend renders riyb, a term used both for military conflict and formal legal disputes, picturing God as both warrior and advocate for the one who cannot defend himself.
Without cause renders chinnam, quoted directly by Jesus in John 15:25 to describe His own rejection by those He came to save.

Gloat and confounded describe the reversal David prays for, that those who rejoiced in his distress would themselves experience shame, a plea for justice rather than a claim of personal authority to enact it.
